headline: Biddeford Pool's Incoming Hour Still Owns July — Bass to 28, Bluefish Chopping Higgins
subhead: A slow dawn at Prouts Neck turned into the best hour of my week once the tide swung into the Pool — here's where the bite's actually happening south of Portland.
body_markdown:
Threw plugs into a dead ocean at Prouts Neck for two hours Tuesday morning and had exactly one swirl to show for it. Southwest wind was light, water looked right, birds were sitting on the rocks doing nothing — and then my phone buzzed with a picture from a buddy fishing the Pool an hour later. Twenty-eight inch bass, fat as a football, taken on a chartreuse Gibbs Danny swimmer right as the tide turned and started pushing into the channel behind the Pool. That's July in Southern Maine in one sentence — you can grind out nothing for hours and then the tide flips and it's a different ocean entirely.

Biddeford Pool on the incoming remains the best hour we get down here, and this week proved it again. The bass are staging out past the bar and riding the flood in through the cut, working the edges where the sand drops into the deeper channel. I've had my best luck fishing that first hour and a half of incoming with a swimming plug — Danny-style or a Bomber Long A in bone or mackerel pattern — worked slow across the current seams. Don't horse it. Let the tide do the swimming for you and just keep the rod tip low, twitching it through the sweep. The fish holding there right now are mostly schoolies and mid-20s, but a couple guys have pulled fish into the high 20s working the last of the night tide before first light, which tells me there's a better class of bass sitting deeper in that hole than what's showing on the surface bite.

Higgins Beach has been the bluefish story all week. Peanut bunker pushed into the wash Sunday and the blues found them fast — proper blitz conditions for about forty minutes on the incoming, birds diving, fish busting bait right in the surf line. If you were there with a topwater popper — a Gibbs Pencil or a Super Strike — you had a stupid-easy hour. I heard from two separate guys who limited out on cocktail blues in that window and one who stuck a bigger fish, six or seven pounds, on a bucktail he happened to have tied on. That bunker school has been moving up and down the beach, not locked into one spot, so if you're headed to Higgins right now, walk the beach and watch for the diving terns before you commit to a spot. When the birds go quiet, so does the bite — it shuts off almost as fast as it turns on.

Pine Point and the Scarborough River marsh have been slower and more of a grind, which is normal for mid-July once the water in there gets skinny and warm on the low. I fished the outgoing there Wednesday evening and picked at schoolie bass working the mouth where the river dumps out past the flats — small profile soft plastics, 4-inch white Slug-Go on a light jighead, worked slow along the channel edge. Nothing big, but steady enough to keep you interested for an hour around sunset. If you want flounder, that same stretch and the channels off Wells Harbor have been giving up decent numbers on bloodworms and squid strips fished on a simple two-hook flounder rig, bounced slow along the mud on the bottom of the tide.

Mackerel showed up off the Wells Harbor jetty and out toward Cape Neddick this week in decent numbers — good sign for the fall run later on, and a great source of fresh bait right now if you want to switch off dead bunker chunks. A Sabiki rig dropped straight down off the jetty rocks on the last two hours of the incoming has been filling coolers fast, and a live mackerel drifted out past the rocks at Prouts Neck or Cape Elizabeth is about as good a bass bait as exists this time of year — I'd rather fish one live mack under a balloon than chuck plugs blind on a slow tide.

Prouts Neck itself has been up and down depending on the wind. When it's blowing out of the southwest like it did Tuesday, that side sets up calm and clean, and the bass push in tight to the rocks on the last two hours of the flood — but you need moving water and the right wind together, and this week we only had one without the other most days. Cape Elizabeth and the water off Ogunquit have stayed quieter than I'd like for mid-July, more grind than blitz, which tells me the bulk of the bigger bass are still holding a little offshore or working the river mouths on darkness rather than committing hard to the open rocks in daylight.

Looking ahead, if the wind holds out of the southwest through the weekend I'd be at Prouts Neck right at first light working a Danny swimmer on the last of the incoming, then sliding down to Biddeford Pool to fish that same tide stage through the cut. If the bunker schools stay put at Higgins, that blitz window is worth building a morning around — just get there early and watch the birds before you commit. Tides are running bigger than they were a couple weeks back, which usually means more water moving through the Pool and better current definition at Prouts — that's the kind of push that turns a decent bass spot into a genuinely good one for a few days.
